stem:
Bulawayo Brick Works makes pallets of bricks. The standard cost card for one pallet and the budget for the month are:

| Standard for one pallet | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Clay: 3.2 tonnes at US\$7.50 a tonne | 24 |
| Labour: 1.75 hours at US\$6.40 an hour | 11.20 |
| Standard selling price | 52 |

Budget: 1,850 pallets and fixed costs of US\$17,400, which are not absorbed into the standard cost.

Actual results for the month:

| Actual | Amount |
| --- | ---: |
| Pallets made and sold | 1,950 |
| Average selling price | US\$50.80 |
| Clay used | 6,420 tonnes costing US\$49,434 |
| Labour | 3,490 hours costing US\$23,732 |
| Fixed costs | US\$18,050 |

A positive variance is favourable (F) and a negative variance is adverse (A). The sales volume variance is valued at the standard contribution per pallet.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the clay variances (amounts only):

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: price

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: usage
parts.explanation: Standard clay = 1,950 × 3.2 = 6,240 tonnes. Used 6,420, 180 more. 180 × US\$7.50 = US\$1,350 A.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the labour variances (amounts only):

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: rate

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: efficiency

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the sales variances (amounts only):

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: price

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: volume

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Prepare a reconciliation of budgeted profit with actual profit.

points.description: Budgeted profit US\$13,680 (1,850 × 16.80 less fixed costs 17,400)
Sales variances: volume 1,680 F and price 2,340 A
Material variances: price 1,284 A and usage 1,350 A
Labour variances: rate 1,396 A and efficiency 496 A
Fixed costs 650 A
Net variance 5,836 A and actual profit US\$7,844

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
| Reconciliation of budgeted and actual profit | Favourable US\$ | Adverse US\$ | US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Budgeted profit |  |  | 13,680 |
| Sales volume variance | 1,680 |  |  |
| Sales price variance |  | 2,340 |  |
| Material price variance |  | 1,284 |  |
| Material usage variance |  | 1,350 |  |
| Labour rate variance |  | 1,396 |  |
| Labour efficiency variance |  | 496 |  |
| Fixed costs over budget |  | 650 |  |
| Net variance (adverse) | 1,680 | 7,516 | (5,836) |

parts.explanation: One mark for each group of lines.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the actual profit from the actual results, as a check on the reconciliation.
parts.explanation: Revenue 99,060 - clay 49,434 - labour 23,732 - fixed costs 18,050 = US\$7,844.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Revenue 99,060 - clay 49,434 - labour 23,732 - fixed costs 18,050 = US\$7,844.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Evaluate the performance of the business for the month and recommend action.

points.description: Profit was US\$5,836 below budget even though 100 more pallets were sold than budgeted
The price cut (US\$2,340 A) cost more than the extra volume gained (US\$1,680 F)
All cost variances are adverse; clay (price and usage) and labour rate are the largest: investigate supplier price, waste and wage rates
Linked causes: poor-quality clay may explain both usage and labour efficiency
Recommendation with a non-financial factor, for example review pricing, find a cheaper supplier or train workers without lowering quality or delivery

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Profit was US\$5,836 below budget. The price cut cost more than the volume gain, and every cost variance was adverse, mainly clay price and usage and labour rate. The business should review its pricing, check the clay supplier and the waste, and train workers, while protecting quality and delivery.

hints: Use two or three of the largest variances.
Link variances, suggest action and mention a non-financial factor.

explanation: This COST25 item calculates direct and sales variances, reconciles budgeted and actual profit and asks for an evaluation with a recommendation.
hints: Standard quantity and hours are for 1,950 pallets.
Standard contribution = selling price less clay and labour.
The reconciliation must agree with the actual profit.

stem:
Masvingo Mills grinds maize meal and sells it in bags. It uses absorption costing and absorbs fixed overhead on direct labour hours. The standard cost and budget are:

| Standard for one bag | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Selling price | 21 |
| Variable cost | 14.20 |
| Fixed overhead absorbed (0.4 labour hours at US\$6.00 an hour) | 2.40 |
| Standard profit | 4.40 |

Budget for the year: 8,000 bags (3,200 labour hours) and fixed overhead of US\$19,200.

Actual results: 7,500 bags were made and sold at an average price of US\$21.60; 3,150 labour hours were worked; fixed overhead was US\$19,900.

A positive variance is favourable (F); a negative variance is adverse (A).

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the sales variances (amounts only):

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: price

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: volume, at standard profit per bag

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the fixed overhead variances (amounts only):

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the standard fixed overhead absorption rate per bag

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: expenditure

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: volume

parts.label: (iv)
parts.stem: capacity

parts.label: (v)
parts.stem: efficiency

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total under-absorption of fixed overhead (amount only).
parts.explanation: Absorbed 18,000 - actual 19,900 = US\$1,900 under-absorbed. Check: expenditure 700 + volume 1,200.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Absorbed 18,000 - actual 19,900 = US\$1,900 under-absorbed. Check: expenditure 700 + volume 1,200.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Prepare a statement showing the overhead absorbed, the actual overhead and how the under-absorption is explained by the variances.

points.description: Overhead absorbed US\$18,000 (7,500 × 2.40) and actual overhead US\$19,900
Under-absorption US\$1,900 adverse
Expenditure US\$700 A and volume US\$1,200 A
Volume split into capacity US\$300 A and efficiency US\$900 A

answerSpec.modelAnswer:

| --- | ---: |
| Overhead absorbed (7,500 bags × US\$2.40) | 18,000 |
| Actual fixed overhead | 19,900 |
| Under-absorbed overhead (adverse) | (1,900) |

parts.explanation: One mark for each group of lines.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Evaluate the performance of the mill, using the sales and fixed overhead variances, and recommend action.

points.description: Sales price is favourable (US\$4,500) but volume is adverse (US\$2,200): fewer bags were sold at a higher price, which suggests a price rise that lost customers
Fixed overhead is under-absorbed by US\$1,900, of which US\$900 is efficiency: the work took 150 hours more than the standard
Capacity is adverse (US\$300) because fewer hours were worked than budgeted, and expenditure is US\$700 over budget
Recommendation: investigate the slow working and the overspending on fixed costs; consider whether the higher price should be kept, and one non-financial factor such as customer loyalty

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The higher price gave US\$4,500 more but 500 fewer bags were sold (US\$2,200 adverse). Fixed overhead was under-absorbed by US\$1,900, mainly because work took 150 hours longer than the standard. The mill should investigate the slow working and the fixed cost overspend and review whether the price rise cost it customers.

hints: Link price and volume; split the volume variance.

explanation: This COST25 item for Cambridge A Level calculates sales and fixed overhead variances and asks for an evaluation.
hints: Standard hours are for the actual output.
Capacity + efficiency should equal volume.
Expenditure + volume should equal the total under-absorption.

stem:
Thandeka Furniture Ltd in Bulawayo is preparing its master budget for the quarter ending 30 June. It plans to sell 2,350 chairs, all on credit, at US\$86 each. Finished goods are valued at the variable cost of US\$49 a chair (materials US\$33, labour US\$12, variable overhead US\$4); there is no other inventory. Finished goods inventory is 130 chairs at the start and 170 chairs at the end. Fixed production overhead is US\$35,400 (including depreciation of US\$8,600), administration and selling expenses US\$20,700 and loan interest US\$1,350. Materials are bought on credit; labour and other costs are paid as incurred. A dividend of US\$5,200 will be paid and equipment costing US\$24,300 will be bought for cash.

| Balances at the start of the quarter | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Non-current assets at cost | 200,300 |
| Accumulated depreciation | 60,600 |
| Finished goods inventory | 6,370 |
| Trade receivables | 21,400 |
| Cash and bank | 8,100 |
| Trade payables (materials only) | 15,700 |
| Share capital | 82,000 |
| Loan (non-current) | 13,500 |

Trade receivables are budgeted to be US\$38,600 and trade payables US\$20,900 at the end of the quarter.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of chairs to be produced.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the budgeted cost of sales.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the budgeted profit for the quarter.
parts.explanation: Gross profit 86,950 - fixed overhead 35,400 - administration 20,700 = 30,850; less interest 1,350 = US\$29,500.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Gross profit 86,950 - fixed overhead 35,400 - administration 20,700 = 30,850; less interest 1,350 = US\$29,500.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the budgeted cash received from customers.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the budgeted cash and bank balance at the end of the quarter.
parts.explanation: Payments: suppliers 73,670 (78,870 + 15,700 - 20,900), labour 28,680, variable overhead 9,560, fixed overhead paid 26,800, administration 20,700, interest 1,350, dividend 5,200, equipment 24,300 = 190,260. Closing bank = 8,100 + 184,900 - 190,260 = US\$2,740.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Payments: suppliers 73,670 (78,870 + 15,700 - 20,900), labour 28,680, variable overhead 9,560, fixed overhead paid 26,800, administration 20,700, interest 1,350, dividend 5,200, equipment 24,300 = 190,260. Closing bank = 8,100 + 184,900 - 190,260 = US\$2,740.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Calculate the total assets at the end of the quarter.
parts.explanation: Non-current assets 139,700 + inventory 8,330 + receivables 38,600 + bank 2,740 = US\$189,370.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Non-current assets 139,700 + inventory 8,330 + receivables 38,600 + bank 2,740 = US\$189,370.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Prepare the budgeted statement of profit or loss for the quarter.

points.description: Heading with the name, statement and period
Revenue 202,100 and cost of sales 115,150
Gross profit 86,950
Fixed production overhead 35,400 and administration 20,700, giving profit from operations 30,850
Finance costs 1,350 and profit for the period 29,500

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Thandeka Furniture Ltd: budgeted statement of profit or loss for the quarter ending 30 June**

|  | US\$ | US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Revenue |  | 202,100 |
| Cost of sales |  | (115,150) |
| **Gross profit** |  | 86,950 |
| Fixed production overhead (including depreciation) | (35,400) |  |
| Administration and selling expenses | (20,700) |  |
| **Profit from operations** |  | 30,850 |
| Finance costs |  | (1,350) |
| **Profit for the period** |  | 29,500 |

parts.explanation: One mark for each group of lines.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Assess whether the plan is satisfactory. Use ratios from the budgeted statements and make a recommendation.

points.description: Gross profit margin is 43.0% and profit from operations gives an ROCE of 18.3% on capital employed of 168,470
The current ratio is 2.38 : 1 and the acid test 1.98 : 1: liquidity looks healthy on paper
But the budgeted bank balance is only US\$2,740, because US\$38,600 is tied up in receivables and cash is used for equipment and the dividend
A fall in sales or slower collection would create an overdraft; recommend arranging an overdraft in advance, collecting faster or reducing the dividend
Non-financial factor, for example customer relationships when chasing payment, or the need for the new equipment
A judgement: acceptable if the cash risk is managed

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Profitability is good (gross margin 43.0%, ROCE 18.3%) and the current ratio of 2.38 : 1 is healthy. However the bank balance is only US\$2,740 because receivables are US\$38,600 and cash is spent on equipment and the dividend. An overdraft should be arranged in advance, collection speeded up or the dividend reduced; the plan is acceptable if the cash risk is managed.

hints: Quote two ratios and the cash balance.

explanation: This COST25 item builds the main figures of a master budget and asks the student to assess the plan.
hints: Cost of sales = 2,350 chairs at the variable cost.
Depreciation is not a cash payment.
The statement of financial position must balance.

stem:
Hatfield Printers in Harare budgeted to print 6,000 jobs in the month at an average price of US\$24.50 a job. The budgeted costs were: materials US\$5.80 a job; labour US\$4.10 a job; variable overhead US\$1.30 a job; maintenance US\$1,800 plus US\$0.45 a job; fixed production overhead US\$15,600; administration US\$8,400.

The business printed 6,700 jobs. Actual results were:

| Actual | US\$ |
| --- | ---: |
| Revenue | 160,100 |
| Materials | 40,100 |
| Labour | 28,300 |
| Variable overhead | 8,950 |
| Maintenance (semi-variable) | 4,950 |
| Fixed production overhead | 15,900 |
| Administration | 8,250 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the flexed budget for:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: materials

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: maintenance

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the flexed budgeted profit.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the actual profit.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the difference between the flexed budgeted profit and the actual profit (amount only).

parts.label: (e)

Flexed materials 38,860, labour 27,470 and variable overhead 8,710 with their variances (all adverse)
Maintenance flexed at 1,800 plus 0.45 per job (4,815) with variance 135 A
Fixed production overhead and administration not flexed, variances 300 A and 150 F
Total costs and profit with the profit variance 6,645 A
Clear column headings and variances labelled F or A

parts.explanation: One mark for each group of lines.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Which line has the largest adverse variance against the flexed budget?
parts.explanation: Revenue is US\$4,050 below the flexed budget.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Evaluate the month's performance and recommend action. Explain why the flexed budget is a better yardstick than the original budget.

points.description: Actual profit (US\$53,650) is above the original budget (US\$51,300) but US\$6,645 below the flexed budget
The original budget ignores the extra 700 jobs, so it flatters the performance; the flexed budget compares like with like
Average price per job was only US\$23.90 (against US\$24.50), which explains the revenue variance of US\$4,050
All variable costs exceeded the flexed budget, especially materials (US\$1,240) and labour (US\$830): investigate waste, supplier prices and overtime
Administration is the only favourable item, but it is small
Recommendation, and a non-financial factor such as quality or customer relations when changing prices or suppliers

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Profit looks better than the original budget only because 700 extra jobs were printed. Against the flexed budget it is US\$6,645 lower. The average price was US\$23.90 instead of US\$24.50 and materials and labour cost more than they should have. The business should review its discounting, the supplier prices and waste, and overtime, while protecting quality and customer relations.

hints: Use two or three of the largest variances.
Explain the choice of yardstick.

explanation: This COST25 item prepares a flexed budget comparison and evaluates the result.

stem:
Chipo Poultry in Chinhoyi is considering a new broiler house costing US\$120,000. The expected net cash inflows are US\$36,000, US\$43,000, US\$48,000, US\$39,000 at the end of years 1 to 4. There is no residual value. The cost of capital is 13%. Discount factors:

| Year | Factor at 13% | Factor at 17% |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 0.885 | 0.855 |
| 2 | 0.783 | 0.731 |
| 3 | 0.693 | 0.624 |
| 4 | 0.613 | 0.534 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the present value of the year 3 inflow at 13%.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the net present value at 13%.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the amount by which the net present value at 17% is below zero (amount only).

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Estimate the internal rate of return by interpolation, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage fall in all inflows that would make the NPV at 13% zero, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: On the NPV rule alone the broiler house should be:

options.content: rejected, because the IRR is above 13%
options.rationale: An IRR above the cost of capital means accept.

options.content: rejected, because the NPV at 17% is negative
options.rationale: The relevant NPV is at the cost of capital, 13%.

options.content: accepted, because the NPV is positive
accepted, because total inflows exceed the outlay
options.rationale: Undiscounted totals are not the NPV rule.

parts.explanation: NPV at the cost of capital is positive, so accept.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Evaluate the project and make a recommendation, using the results of this question and referring to risk and one non-financial factor.

points.description: NPV at 13% is US\$2,700 positive and the IRR of 14.1% is above the 13% cost of capital: accept on both methods
The margin is very small: a fall of only 2.2% in the inflows would remove the NPV
Poultry prices, feed costs and disease make the forecasts uncertain, especially in later years
The IRR is an interpolated estimate and the NPV depends on the cost of capital chosen
A higher cost of capital (17%) gives a negative NPV, so the decision is sensitive to the rate
Non-financial factor, for example employment and supply of chicks to local markets, biosecurity or the fit with the farm's strategy
A clear recommendation with conditions, for example proceed only if buyers' contracts reduce the risk, or seek further evidence

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The NPV is positive at 13% and the IRR of 14.1% exceeds the cost of capital, so the project passes both tests. However the margin is tiny (2.2%), the forecasts are uncertain (prices, feed, disease) and at 17% the NPV is negative. The farm should proceed only if buyers' contracts reduce the risk, and should also consider biosecurity, employment and fit with its strategy.

parts.explanation: One mark for each point, up to 7.
hints: Quote the NPV and IRR, the margin of safety, risk, a non-financial factor and a decision.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: State two limitations of using net present value to appraise this project.

points.description: It depends on forecasts of inflows that are uncertain, especially in later years
The result depends on the cost of capital chosen, which is an estimate
Non-financial factors are ignored
It is harder for managers to understand than payback

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: NPV depends on uncertain forecasts of inflows and on an estimated cost of capital. It also ignores non-financial factors.

parts.explanation: Two limitations, each with a brief explanation: 2 marks each.

explanation: This COST25 item calculates NPVs at two rates, estimates the IRR, tests sensitivity and asks for a recommendation.
hints: Multiply each inflow by its factor.
The NPV at 13% is the decision measure; the IRR is interpolated between 13% and 17%.

stem:
Mutare Bakery can buy one of two machines, Machine P or Machine Q. Each costs US\$94,000 and has no residual value. Net cash inflows arise evenly during each year.

| Net cash inflows (US\$) | Machine P | Machine Q |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Year 1 | 27,500 | 50,500 |
| Year 2 | 35,500 | 37,500 |
| Year 3 | 41,500 | 24,500 |
| Year 4 | 29,000 | - |

The bakery requires a payback of at most 2.5 years and an accounting rate of return (ARR) of at least 15%.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the payback period of Machine P, in years to two decimal places.
parts.explanation: After 2 years 63,000 is recovered; 31,000 remains. 31,000 ÷ 41,500 = 0.75. Payback = 2.75 years.
parts.workedSolution: 1. After 2 years 63,000 is recovered; 31,000 remains. 31,000 ÷ 41,500 = 0.75. Payback = 2.75 years.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the payback period of Machine Q, in years to two decimal places.
parts.explanation: After 2 years 88,000 is recovered; 6,000 remains. 6,000 ÷ 24,500 = 0.24. Payback = 2.24 years.
parts.workedSolution: 1. After 2 years 88,000 is recovered; 6,000 remains. 6,000 ÷ 24,500 = 0.24. Payback = 2.24 years.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Machine P pays back in 2 years and some months. How many months after the 2 full years (to the nearest month)?
parts.explanation: 0.747 of a year × 12 = 9.0, so 9 months. Payback is 2 years 9 months.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 0.747 of a year × 12 = 9.0, so 9 months. Payback is 2 years 9 months.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the ARR of Machine P, to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: Total profit = 133,500 - 94,000 = 39,500; average = 9,875; average investment = 47,000. ARR = 21.0%.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Total profit = 133,500 - 94,000 = 39,500; average = 9,875; average investment = 47,000. ARR = 21.0%.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the ARR of Machine Q, to one decimal place.
parts.explanation: Total profit = 112,500 - 94,000 = 18,500; average over 3 years = 6,166.67; average investment 47,000. ARR = 13.1%.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Total profit = 112,500 - 94,000 = 18,500; average over 3 years = 6,166.67; average investment 47,000. ARR = 13.1%.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Calculate the total profit over the life of:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Machine P

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Machine Q

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Which statement about the two machines is correct?

options.rationale: P's payback is 2.75 years, above 2.5, and Q's ARR is 13.1%, below 15%.
P's ARR and Q's payback both meet their requirements.

options.content: P meets the payback requirement and Q the ARR requirement
options.rationale: It is the other way round.

options.content: Q meets payback but not ARR; P meets ARR but not payback

parts.explanation: P: payback fails, ARR passes. Q: payback passes, ARR fails.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Evaluate the two machines and recommend which to buy.

points.description: Q pays back faster (2.24 against 2.75 years) and meets the 2.5-year requirement; P does not
P has the higher ARR (21.0% against 13.1%) and earns more than twice the total profit (US\$39,500 against US\$18,500); Q fails the ARR target
Neither machine meets both targets, so the choice depends on priorities: liquidity and risk favour Q; total return favours P
Payback ignores cash flows after the payback point and the time value of money, and ARR uses profits and ignores timing
P's longer life means later flows are less certain; Q's profits are lower in total
A discounted measure such as NPV would give a better comparison; the cost of capital is needed
A clear recommendation with a non-financial factor, for example reliability of the machine or the effect on staff

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Machine Q pays back within 2.5 years but earns only 13.1%; Machine P earns 21.0% and more than twice the total profit but pays back in 2.75 years. Neither meets both targets. If cash is short and risk matters, Q is safer; if the bakery can wait, P earns more. NPV would give a better comparison. On these figures Machine P is the better investment unless the bakery is short of cash, subject to reliability.

parts.explanation: One mark for each point, up to 7.
hints: Compare each machine with both requirements.
Mention the weaknesses of the methods.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Explain why the payback method is useful to a business with little cash.

points.description: It shows how quickly the outlay is recovered
A short payback reduces the time the cash is at risk
The recovered cash can be reinvested or used to repay loans sooner

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Payback shows how soon the cash comes back, which reduces risk and frees money for other uses when cash is short.

explanation: This COST25 item calculates payback and ARR for two machines and asks for an evaluation against targets.
hints: Use cumulative inflows for payback.
ARR = average profit ÷ (outlay ÷ 2).
